lesson.title: Green Light, Red Light: Start and Stop Codons
lesson.summary: AUG is the near-universal start codon that marks where translation begins and sets the reading frame, while three stop codons, lacking any matching tRNA, signal a release factor to end the polypeptide chain.
lesson.body:
Among the sixty-four possible codons, one plays a special dual role. AUG is the start codon, marking the position in an mRNA where a ribosome begins translating, and it also happens to code for the amino acid methionine. Because of this overlap, nearly every newly made protein in a eukaryotic cell begins its life with methionine at what will become its N-terminal end, though that methionine is sometimes removed afterward by other cellular machinery. Choosing the correct AUG to start at matters enormously, because once the ribosome commits to a starting position, it reads every codon after it in unbroken groups of three, with no gaps and no overlap. Get the starting point wrong by even a single nucleotide, and every codon downstream is read in the wrong grouping, an error called a frameshift that scrambles the entire rest of the protein.

To get that starting position right, cells use a dedicated initiator tRNA, distinct from the ordinary tRNA that carries methionine to internal AUG codons later in the message. This initiator tRNA is specifically recognized by initiation factors during the first step of translation, a detail that becomes important in the next chapter's overview of how translation actually begins.

At the other end of the process, translation has to know when to stop, and three codons handle that job: UAA, UAG, and UGA. Unlike every other codon, none of these three code for an amino acid, and the reason is structural rather than arbitrary: there is no tRNA in the cell whose anticodon pairs with any of them. When one of these stop codons enters the ribosome's A site, no tRNA arrives to fill it. Instead, a protein called a release factor binds there, and that binding triggers the release of the completed polypeptide chain from the final tRNA, followed by disassembly of the translation complex. Taken together, sixty-one of the sixty-four possible codons code for an amino acid, three act purely as stop signals, and AUG does double duty as both the start signal and the codon for methionine.
